mcqs.q: Research ethics is best defined as:
opts: Systematic application of moral principles to the design and conduct of research
The set of laws that punish researchers who harm participants
The statistical methods used to avoid bias within a study
The process of obtaining a signature on a consent form
mcqs.explain: It applies to research involving people, identifiable data, human biological material, communities, and where relevant animals and the environment.

mcqs.q: The two linked questions that ethics asks are:
opts: Can it produce valuable knowledge, and are participants treated fairly and protected?
Is the study funded, and will the results be published?
Is the sample size adequate, and is the analysis correct?
Is the researcher qualified, and is the institution accredited?
mcqs.explain: Both must be answered; a scientifically worthless study is an ethical problem because it exposes participants for nothing.

mcqs.q: Which statement best reflects the role of ethical review?
opts: Ethical review is not a barrier to research; it is a safeguard for participants and science
Ethical review is an administrative delay that research must tolerate
Ethical review replaces the need for informed consent
Ethical review applies only to drug trials
mcqs.explain: It also improves the quality of the science by forcing careful design, transparency and accountability.

mcqs.q: Research ethics protects participants from all the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: The listed risks are physical, psychological, social, financial, privacy and legal.

mcqs.q: Which is a listed importance of research ethics that concerns the SCIENCE rather than the participant?
opts: Improves scientific quality through careful methods, transparency and accountability
mcqs.explain: Ensuring research is useful and well designed is the other science-facing point among the five.

mcqs.q: The major international reference for medical research involving human participants is the:
mcqs.explain: It covers human participants, identifiable human data and human biological material.

mcqs.q: In addition to international declarations, the researcher must:
opts: Always check the regulations of the country and institution where the study will occur
Follow only the rules of the journal where the paper will be published
Rely on the supervisor's personal judgement
mcqs.explain: International declarations set the floor; local law and institutional policy may require more.

mcqs.q: The principle that participants make a free and informed choice and can leave the study at any time is:
mcqs.explain: Beneficence is maximizing benefits and minimizing harm.

mcqs.q: The principle of beneficence requires the researcher to:
opts: Maximize benefits and minimize harm to participants
mcqs.explain: Fair selection is justice; honesty is integrity; protecting information is privacy and confidentiality.

mcqs.q: Ensuring fair selection and treatment of participants and fair sharing of benefits and risks is the principle of:
mcqs.explain: Social responsibility is that research should benefit society and contribute positively to the community.

mcqs.q: Being honest, accurate and transparent throughout the research is the principle of:
mcqs.explain: It underpins the prohibition of fabrication, falsification and selective reporting.

mcqs.q: Which group is given as an example of a vulnerable population requiring extra protection?
opts: Children and people with cognitive impairments
mcqs.explain: Protection of vulnerable groups is one of the seven principles.

mcqs.q: The principle that research should benefit society and contribute positively to the community is:
mcqs.explain: Justice concerns fairness among participants; social responsibility looks outward to the community.

mcqs.q: The Research Ethics Committee or IRB reviews the study:
opts: Before it starts, to make sure it is scientifically sound and ethically acceptable
After data collection but before analysis
mcqs.explain: Data collected before approval is generally unusable, and many journals require an approval number.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a listed function of the IRB?
opts: Performing the statistical analysis of the collected data
Checking risks and benefits and how participants are chosen and recruited
Checking how consent will be obtained and how privacy will be protected
Reviewing the use of AI, including data sources, security measures and human supervision
mcqs.explain: The IRB also produces the IRB number of approval.

mcqs.q: Regarding AI, the IRB specifically reviews:
opts: Data sources, security measures, and human supervision
Only the brand of AI tool used
Only whether AI was used at all
Nothing — AI is outside the IRB remit
mcqs.explain: AI use must also be disclosed transparently by the researcher.

mcqs.q: Informed consent is best described as:
opts: A process supporting a voluntary, informed decision — more than a signature
A signed legal document protecting the institution
A formality required only in drug trials
A record that the participant was told the study title
mcqs.explain: The participant needs understandable information and adequate time.

mcqs.q: Which must be explained to the participant during the consent process?
opts: Randomization, possible risks, potential benefits, privacy protections and withdrawal
Only the potential benefits of the study
Only the funding source of the study
Only the name of the principal investigator
mcqs.explain: Participants may refuse or withdraw without penalty or loss of entitled clinical care.

mcqs.q: A participant who withdraws from a study:
opts: Faces no penalty and does not lose entitled clinical care
Must pay back any reimbursement received
Loses access to the routine treatment they were entitled to
Must give a written justification to the IRB
mcqs.explain: This is a direct expression of respect for autonomy.

mcqs.q: Written consent is the standard type used for:
opts: Most clinical trials and higher-risk research
mcqs.explain: It is a signed form completed after explaining the study.

mcqs.q: Verbal consent is an oral agreement documented by the researcher, used:
opts: In low-risk studies or when signing is not appropriate, for example a telephone interview
Only when the participant cannot read
mcqs.explain: The level of risk determines which type of consent is acceptable.

mcqs.q: Completing a survey or clicking “I agree” is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Implied consent is acceptable only for minimal-risk research such as an online survey.

mcqs.q: When a participant cannot consent for themselves, for example a child or an adult lacking capacity:
opts: A parent or legal representative consents on their behalf
The researcher may proceed without consent
The IRB signs the consent form
mcqs.explain: Vulnerable participants also require extra protection and care.

mcqs.q: Participants mistaking research for medical treatment is called:
mcqs.explain: It arises when consent wording implies the participant is receiving better care rather than taking part in research.

mcqs.q: Participants feeling pressured to join a study is:
mcqs.explain: It is especially likely when the recruiter has power over the participant, such as a professor who assigns grades.

mcqs.q: Personal or financial interests that may influence the research constitute:
mcqs.explain: It is one of the common ethical issues in clinical and health research.

mcqs.q: The ethical issue in which participants may not receive effective treatment, potentially causing harm, is:
mcqs.explain: It must be weighed against beneficence — maximize benefits, minimize harm.

mcqs.q: Reporting favorable results selectively, or unfair authorship, is listed as:
mcqs.explain: Selective reporting makes the findings look different from the truth and so also breaches integrity.

mcqs.q: Which is listed among AI-related ethical problems?
opts: Bias, inaccurate or fake references, data security risks, or failure to disclose AI use
mcqs.explain: These are the AI-related problems specified among the common ethical issues.

mcqs.q: Making up data, results, or information that was never collected is:
mcqs.explain: Falsification, by contrast, changes data that did exist.

mcqs.q: Changing, manipulating, or deleting data so the results look different from the truth is:
mcqs.explain: Fabrication invents data that never existed; falsification alters real data.

mcqs.q: Using someone else's ideas, words, or work without giving proper credit is:
mcqs.explain: It is one of the four listed forms of scientific misconduct.

mcqs.q: Using AI to create fake references, data, images, or research results and presenting them as real is:
opts: AI misuse, a form of scientific misconduct
An acceptable use of AI if disclosed
Only a problem if the paper is published
mcqs.explain: The four forms of misconduct are fabrication, falsification, plagiarism and AI misuse.

mcqs.q: The AI principle requiring researchers to clearly disclose how AI was used is:
mcqs.explain: Accountability means the researcher remains responsible for accuracy and quality.

mcqs.q: The principle that researchers remain responsible for the accuracy and quality of the work, whatever tool was used, is:
mcqs.explain: Responsibility cannot be transferred to the AI tool.

mcqs.q: Regarding privacy and security in AI use, researchers should:
opts: Protect confidential and identifiable data and not upload sensitive information to AI tools
Upload data freely as long as names are removed
Upload data only to paid AI services
Upload data if the study has IRB approval
mcqs.explain: Removing names does not make data anonymous when ages, diagnoses, dates and notes remain.

mcqs.q: AI should be treated as:
opts: A supportive tool, not a substitute for independent thinking
mcqs.explain: Human oversight is required: AI cannot replace ethical judgment, supervision, or clinical responsibility.

mcqs.q: Which is an APPROPRIATE use of AI in research?
opts: Suggesting statistical analysis code, which researchers must test and review themselves
Generating references without checking whether the articles exist
Uploading identifiable patient records for analysis
Producing results when the real data are unavailable
mcqs.explain: Every appropriate use keeps the researcher in control and verifying.

mcqs.q: AI may help organize research articles and summarize information provided that:
opts: The information is verified from the original sources
The summary is at least 200 words
The AI tool is cited as an author
The summary is not used in the discussion section
mcqs.explain: Unverified AI output crosses into AI misuse.

mcqs.q: A professor recruits students from their own class, tells them participation shows commitment, requires named consent forms, and also assigns their final grades. The MAIN ethical problem is:
opts: Undue influence and a conflict of interest that undermine voluntary consent
Failure to use a validated questionnaire
mcqs.explain: Named forms also breach confidentiality, since the grader can see exactly who declined.

mcqs.q: A student uploads a file of patient ages, diagnoses, appointment dates, medications and notes to a public AI chatbot, with names removed. This is unacceptable mainly because:
opts: The remaining details can re-identify patients, so the data are not truly anonymous
AI chatbots cannot analyse clinical data accurately
The file was too large for the tool
Only supervisors are allowed to use AI
mcqs.explain: It breaches the privacy and security principle and was not covered by consent or IRB approval.

mcqs.q: A consent form for an experimental AI symptom-assessment tool says it will help doctors provide better care, but omits that the system is experimental, may make mistakes, and that normal care is available. This is an example of:
opts: Therapeutic misconception caused by incomplete consent
mcqs.explain: Consent must explain possible risks, the experimental nature, alternatives, and the right to refuse without penalty.

saqs.q: Define research ethics and state the two questions it asks.
saqs.a: RESEARCH ETHICS — the systematic application of moral principles and professional standards to the design, conduct, review and reporting of research. It covers research involving people, identifiable data, human biological material, communities, and where relevant animals and the environment. The two questions: can this study produce valuable knowledge, and are participants treated fairly and protected from avoidable harm? Ethical review is a safeguard, not a barrier.

ans.text: The systematic application of moral principles and professional standards to the design, conduct, review and reporting of research — covering people, identifiable data, human biological material, communities, and where relevant animals and the environment.

list: Are participants treated fairly and protected from avoidable harm?

ans.text: Ethical review is not a barrier to research — it is a safeguard for participants and for science.

saqs.q: Discuss the importance of research ethics.
saqs.a: Protects participants from physical, psychological, social, financial, privacy and legal risks · respects rights, dignity, safety, autonomy and privacy · builds public trust · ensures research is useful and well-designed, avoiding unnecessary risk · improves scientific quality through careful methods, transparency and accountability. The Declaration of Helsinki is the major international reference, but always check national and institutional regulations.

list: Protects participants from physical, psychological, social, financial, privacy and legal risks
Respects rights, dignity, safety, autonomy and privacy
Builds public trust in research and healthcare
Ensures research is useful and well-designed, avoiding unnecessary risks
Improves scientific quality — careful methods, transparency and accountability

ans.text: The Declaration of Helsinki is a major international reference for medical research involving human participants, identifiable data and biological material — but always check the regulations of the country and institution where the study will occur.

saqs.q: List and explain the principles of research ethics.
saqs.a: RESPECT FOR AUTONOMY — free informed choice, free to leave at any time. BENEFICENCE — maximize benefit, minimize harm. JUSTICE — fair selection and treatment, fair sharing of benefits and risks. INTEGRITY — honest, accurate, transparent. PRIVACY AND CONFIDENTIALITY — protect personal information. PROTECTION OF VULNERABLE GROUPS — extra care for children, cognitive impairment. SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY — research should benefit society.

head: Principle
Meaning
rows: participants make a free and informed choice and can leave at any time
fair selection and treatment, and fair sharing of benefits and risks
extra protection for children or people with cognitive impairment
research should benefit society and contribute positively to the community

saqs.q: Describe the functions and responsibilities of Research Ethics Committees / IRBs.
saqs.a: The REC/IRB reviews the study BEFORE it starts, to ensure it is scientifically sound and ethically acceptable. It checks risks and benefits, how participants are chosen and recruited, how consent will be obtained, and how privacy and confidentiality are protected. It reviews AI use — data sources, security, human supervision. And it produces the IRB number of approval.

list: Reviews the study before it starts — ensuring it is scientifically sound and ethically acceptable
Checks how participants are chosen and recruited
Checks how privacy and confidentiality will be protected
Reviews the use of AI — data sources, security measures and human supervision

saqs.q: Explain informed consent and list its types.
saqs.a: Consent supports a voluntary informed decision — more than a signature. The participant needs understandable information and adequate time; the researcher explains randomization, risks, benefits, privacy and withdrawal; participants may refuse or withdraw without penalty or loss of entitled care. TYPES — written (signed form, most trials and higher-risk), verbal (documented orally, low-risk or telephone), implied (completing a survey or clicking 'I agree', minimal-risk only), and by parent or legal representative (children, adults lacking capacity).

ans.text: Consent supports a voluntary, informed decision — it is more than a signature. The participant needs understandable information and adequate time; the researcher must explain randomization, risks, benefits, privacy protections and withdrawal. Participants may refuse or withdraw without penalty or loss of entitled clinical care.

saqs.q: Discuss the common ethical issues in clinical and health research.
saqs.a: THERAPEUTIC MISCONCEPTION — mistaking research for treatment. UNDUE INFLUENCE — pressure to join. PRIVACY FAILURES. CONFLICTS OF INTEREST. PLACEBO OR WITHHOLDING TREATMENT — potential harm. SELECTIVE REPORTING AND AUTHORSHIP. AI-RELATED PROBLEMS — bias, fake references, data security, undisclosed use.

participants may not receive effective treatment — potentially causing harm
favourable results reported selectively, or authorship unfair
bias · inaccurate or fake references · data security risks · failure to disclose AI use

saqs.q: Define the forms of scientific misconduct.
saqs.a: FABRICATION — making up data, results or information never collected. FALSIFICATION — changing, manipulating or deleting data so results look different from the truth. PLAGIARISM — using someone else's ideas, words or work without proper credit. AI MISUSE — using AI to create fake references, data, images or results and presenting them as real.

Definition

using AI to create fake references, data, images or results and presenting them as real

saqs.q: Discuss the principles of AI use in research and give appropriate uses of AI.
saqs.a: PRINCIPLES — transparency (disclose how AI was used), accountability (researchers remain responsible), privacy and security (never upload sensitive data), responsible use (a supportive tool, not a substitute for thinking), human oversight (AI cannot replace ethical judgement, supervision or clinical responsibility). APPROPRIATE USES — developing research questions; improving writing and organization; creating study plans, teaching materials and interview questions; suggesting statistical code, which must be tested and reviewed; organizing and summarizing articles, verified from the original sources.

protect confidential and identifiable data — do not upload sensitive information
treat AI as a supportive tool, not a substitute for independent thinking
AI cannot replace ethical judgement, supervision or clinical responsibility

Improving writing, grammar, clarity and organization — the researcher staying in control
Creating study plans, teaching materials and interview questions
